newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity settles mostly lower on weather.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity settles mostly lower on weather.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures settled mostly lower Wednesday on forecasts of cool, wet weather in the Southwest and rising spot supply due to unit returns and pending capacity increase on the Pacific Intertie.

The latest six to 10 day forecasts showed the West would experience seasonal to slightly cooler-than-seasonal readings regionwide with a monsoonal flow bringing above-normal precipitation in the mountainous areas.
Asked about the reason behind an afternoon rebound in August COB futures, a Houston futures trader said, "The only thing that's keeping it up is cash prices."
The Northwest physical market was lifted by no surplus next-day offer from Bonneville Power Administration and slower flows through regional hydroelectric projects.
Firm, peak power deliveries for Thursday at COB rose about two dollars to $19.00-21.50 a MWh, while those at PV fell three dollars to $32.00-34.00.
September California-Oregon Border (COB) futures settled up two cents at $22.50 after hitting a low of $22.10.
October COB finished down 30 cents at $21.40. Deferred COB contracts ended one to 35 cents lower.
September Palo Verde (PV) settled down 59 cents at $29.18 a MWh after traded between $28.85 and $29.60.
October PV finished down 85 cents at $22.25. Other PV months ended down 35 to up five cents.
While the complex will likely trend lower, market sources said players are reluctant to go either long or short heading into the new month.
"People are just playing defense right now," a East Coast futures trader said.
Discharge from the 6,150 MW Grand Coulee hydropower dam, the uppermost U.S. project on the Columbia River, were being slowed, meaning less power generation through Monday.

Three western power units--a 260 MW Hayden coal-fired unit in Colorado, a 550 MW Jim Bridger coal-fired unit in Wyoming, and a 600 MW Grand Coulee hydroturbine in Washington--were set to resume operations today after unplanned repairs.
Meanwhile, another 550 MW Jim Bridger unit was shut today due to overheating. No restart date has been set.
The 254 MW unit 1 at the Valmy coal-fired power plant in Nevada will likely be off line for a week after being shut Monday due to a rotor problem.
The 750 MW Four Corners coal-fired unit 5 in New Mexico, shut earlier this month to repair a high pressure generator field, was planned to restart next week.
The 1,221 MW Palo Verde 2 nuclear power unit in Arizona began slowly coasting down to its September refueling outage.

Capacity on the Pacific Intertie transmission system, the main conduit moving cheap Northwest hydropower to southern California, should be raised by 600 megawatts (MW) to 6,900 MW no later than Monday.

The Intertie's current 6,300 MW rating will expire Thursday, but the limit would likely be extended if the new 6,900 MW rating is not implemented by then, the Western Systems Coordinating Council said.
((--R Leong, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1622))
